newsitem.title: INDIA: India aims to deregulate electricity pricing.
newsitem.headline: India aims to deregulate electricity pricing.

text.p: India is considering handing over the setting of electricity tariffs to autonomous agencies in a bid to speed up deregulation of the industry, a senior official said on Thursday.

Rakesh Kakkar, a joint secretary in the Power Ministry, told a meeting of the Independent Power Producers Association of India (IPPAI) that a bill aimed at setting up regional regulatory commissions would be introduced during the federal parliament session due to start next week.

"At the heart of all problems is the poor finances of the state electricity boards (SEBs)," Kakkar told the meeting. "Tariffs and tariff structures (fixed by state governments) have debilitated the viability of SEBs. In the sale of electricity, the government must be taken away from pricing decisions."

Huge losses run up by the SEBs are a major reason for power producers seeking payback assurances from India's state governments through power purchase agreements -- a key issue over which projects have been delayed.
India's demand for electricity is growing at nine percent a year and government officials say it needs to generate 142,000 megawatts by 2007 against the present capacity of 83,288 megawatts.

A committee set up to assess the energy requirement during 1997-2002 has estimated demand will touch 569 billion kilowatt hours requiring a capacity addition of 57,734 megawatts. Out of the total capacity addition, the private sector's contribution is pegged at 28,244 megawatts.

Kakkar stressed the need to liberalise distribution and pricing controls over coal and liquid fuel. "Fuel supply, another area where power projects get bogged down, should be taken out of government control," he said.
"While coal is a pure monopoly of the government, liquid fuel is a virtual monopoly. It is necessary to take these markets away from the government," Kakkar added.

IPPAI president P.K. Sen also called for the removal of subsidies from the tariff structure. "Subsidies have distorted the supply and distribution of electricity and lack of accountability has made the SEBs sick," he said.
He welcomed the government's intention to set up independent regulatory bodies but urged that the commissions be impartial and outside the influence of political motives.
The IPPAI is an association of 30 companies which produce a total of 20,000 megawatts.
